title: FlashInfer: Efficient and Customizable Attention Engine for LLM Inference Serving
problem: LLM inference serving requires attention kernels that simultaneously handle heterogeneous KV-cache storage layouts (ragged, paged, tree-structured), diverse attention variants (GQA, MLA, sliding-window), and dynamic request batching, while remaining compatible with static CUDAGraph capture.
motivation: Existing attention kernels (FlashAttention, Triton-based backends) are optimized for a single storage format and static batch shapes; adapting them to production serving workloads with shared prefixes, paged memory, and mixed request types requires significant rewriting and yields suboptimal memory access and load imbalance.
method: FlashInfer unifies different KV-cache layouts—ragged, paged, and tree-structured—through a single Block-Sparse Row (BSR) format, allowing all layouts to use the same computation path. It decomposes attention calculations into shared-prefix and unique-suffix portions, combining partial softmax results to reuse work across requests. For each attention variant (GQA, MLA, sliding-window), a JIT compiler generates optimized CUDA code templates once on first request, then reuses the compiled binaries for all subsequent requests. Finally, a load-balanced scheduler distributes computation work to GPU thread blocks using a priority queue, wrapped in a static layer to remain compatible with CUDAGraph (static CUDA execution graphs).
key_novelty: FlashInfer solves the problem of diverse KV-cache layouts by introducing a single Block-Sparse Row format that represents ragged, paged, and tree-structured layouts uniformly, while maintaining compatibility with CUDAGraph (static GPU execution graphs) through a static priority queue wrapper that enables dynamic load balancing.
contributions: Block-sparse row format unifying heterogeneous KV-cache layouts for attention computation
Composable formats enabling shared-prefix decomposition and partial softmax merging
JIT compiler for on-demand attention kernel instantiation across GQA, MLA, and sliding-window variants
Load-balanced CUDAGraph-compatible scheduling algorithm using priority-queue tile assignment
Integration into SGLang, vLLM, and MLC-Engine with measured end-to-end speedups

metrics.ITL_reduction_vs_triton: 29-69% inter-token latency reduction vs compiler backends on LLM serving benchmarks
metrics.parallel_generation_speedup: 13-17% speedup for LLM serving with parallel generation

limitations: JIT compilation adds first-request latency; warm-up required for production deployment
BSR block size must be tuned per hardware; sub-optimal block sizes degrade performance
Load-balanced scheduling overhead may dominate for very short sequences
Composable format merging requires storing intermediate partial softmax states, increasing SRAM pressure
